blocks.text: Ashcombe Advisory Partners

Ashcombe Advisory Partners is a corporate communications and investor relations advisory. We work with mid-market public companies, and with private companies preparing for a public listing, on how they explain themselves to investors and analysts, to the financial press, and to their own people.

This overview describes what we do, how we run an engagement, and who does the work. It is intended for companies weighing whether we are the right adviser for them, and we have tried to set the practice out plainly.
The work we are asked to do

Most of our work begins with a particular moment: an earnings release, a change in leadership, a transaction, a regulatory filing, or a question from the market that a company would prefer to answer once and answer well. We help the company decide what it can say, what it ought to say, and in what order, and we draft the material that carries the message.

We give the same care to what follows an announcement. An analyst's first question, a reporter's follow-up, or an employee's reasonable concern will usually arrive within hours, and in our view the answers should be settled before the announcement goes out.
Areas of practice
Our advice is organized around the lines of work below. In practice they overlap, and a single engagement will often draw on more than one of them.

items: Corporate positioning: the account of a company's strategy and prospects that management, the board, and the investor materials can all hold to consistently.
Investor relations programs: earnings materials, management talking points, analyst and investor outreach, and the preparation that precedes a call.
Media relations programs: planning and preparing a company's dealings with the business and trade press, including interviews, briefings, and the handling of inbound inquiries.
Executive messaging: the remarks, letters, and prepared answers that a chief executive or chief financial officer delivers in his or her own name.
Crisis communications: advice when a matter becomes public before a company is ready to speak to it, with close attention to what can be stated accurately at each stage.

Reputation audits: a structured review of how a company is presently understood by investors, the press, and its employees, and of where that understanding departs from the company's own account of itself.

blocks.text: How an engagement runs

Each engagement opens with a signed engagement letter and a kickoff memo recording the scope, the people involved on both sides, and the decisions the client reserves to itself. From there the work is conducted largely by email: drafts circulate, approvals are given or withheld, and the timeline is managed in a thread that everyone on the engagement can see.

We keep formal documents to the few that serve a purpose. A client may expect prompt and brief replies from us, a clear record of what was approved and by whom, and an assurance that nothing we have drafted will reach the market without the client's express sign-off.
The people involved

Julie Hill, Managing Partner, leads the firm and reads every client announcement before it is released. She came to advisory work from corporate investor relations, and she tends to read a draft first as an analyst on an earnings call would hear it.

Christopher Walton, Senior Advisor, spent the early part of his career in financial journalism. He edits with a reporter's attention to headlines and opening paragraphs, and he will tell a client, courteously, when a preferred phrase is unlikely to survive the first question put to it.

Lisa Flores, Director of Operations, is responsible for engagement paperwork, billing, and scheduling, and for the systems that allow a small firm to keep its commitments. Pamela Rojas, Office Manager, keeps our files and shared mailbox in order and is generally the quickest route to a document or a meeting time. Alongside them is a bench of advisors, associates, and analysts who carry the day-to-day work of each engagement.
Confidentiality

We do not publish the names of the companies we advise. A company is entitled to decide for itself whether, and when, to say that it has retained an adviser, and this overview describes our work in general terms for that reason.
Beginning a conversation

A company considering an engagement is welcome to write to Lisa Flores, who will arrange an initial conversation with Julie Hill and, where it would be useful, with the advisor likely to lead the work.
All,

A small request concerning the conference room. Twice last week the room was held informally by one of us while someone else had already entered the same hour on the shared calendar, and on both occasions a meeting began late as a result. From now on I would ask that we treat the calendar as the only record of who has the room, and that a booking be entered there before the time is offered to anyone outside the firm.
If you hold a standing meeting that is not yet on the calendar, please add it before the end of this week so that the record is complete.
Thanks
Hi Michael and Pamela,

I will be out of the office on Monday and Tuesday of next week for a family commitment, and I will be back at my desk on Wednesday morning. I will read email each evening, but anything that cannot wait should go to Michael in the meantime.

Pamela, the Tuesday afternoon room booking held in my name can be released, and I would like the small conference room for an hour on Wednesday morning instead, so that the three of us can go through the rest of the month. Michael, could you tell Pamela by Thursday whether Wednesday at ten works for you, so that she can put it on the calendar?
Sincerely
Welcome: Amy Carter, Communications Associate

We are pleased to record that Amy Carter has joined Ashcombe Advisory Partners as a Communications Associate in the Advisory group. This note, prepared by Julie Hill, sets out her role, where she sits in the practice, and what has been agreed for her first weeks, so that the file reflects what she has been told.

Amy will draft investor-facing materials for our clients: talking points for management, the supporting language for earnings and other announcements, and the questions and answers that travel with them. She reports to Michael Morris, Partner, who runs the advisory bench day to day and will decide which client relationships she joins and in what sequence.

An associate's drafts sit close to the claims a client wishes to make, and they are often the first place where an overstatement can be caught. We would ask Amy to raise a question about a draft whenever she has one, and preferably before she begins it; in our experience that habit saves a round of revisions more often than not.
For the first period, we have agreed the following arrangements:

items: Before she drafts for any engagement, Amy will read its file in order, beginning with the engagement letter and kickoff memo and then the correspondence, so that she knows what the client has already approved.
Her drafts go to Michael Morris for review before they are shared with a client, and nothing she prepares will go to a client without that review.
The operations team will arrange her building access, laptop, and email account, and will take her through the shared drive and the firm's filing conventions.
Client drafts and the timing of announcements are confidential until the client releases them, and are not discussed outside the people working on the engagement.
Time is recorded against each engagement at the end of every working day.
She is welcome to sit in on the internal review of announcements, which is the quickest way to learn how the firm reads a draft.

blocks.text: Her first scheduled step is a working session with Michael Morris early next week, at which they will agree the matters she will join first.
New Staff Record

We are glad to welcome Sandra Mcdonald to the firm. She takes up the Client Coordinator position in Operations, a role that exists so that the scheduling, travel, and practical arrangements around our client meetings rest with one person who can see all of them at once.

Sandra will coordinate calendars across the advisory bench, arrange travel, and manage the logistics of client meetings, from rooms and materials to the confirmations that go out beforehand. She will also be the first point of contact for a client's office when a meeting needs to be arranged or moved. Where two calendars disagree, we would ask her to resolve the difference with the people concerned and to confirm the outcome in writing, since a meeting entered at one time on one calendar and at another time on a second is the most common way for a small office to miss a commitment.

During her first weeks Sandra will work alongside the operations team to learn the shared calendar, the shared mailbox, and the firm's filing conventions, and building access and a firm email account will be ready for her first day. Questions about the firm's systems or paperwork should go to Lisa Flores in the first instance. We do not expect her to take sole charge of any advisor's schedule until she has seen how each of them works, and Lisa Flores will decide the pace at which that responsibility passes to her.
Her first step is a review of the advisory calendars with Lisa Flores, at which the two of them will agree the order in which Sandra takes each one on.
Dear Michelle,

The building management office has told us that the lobby doors will be on card access only from tomorrow evening through the end of the holiday weekend, and when I compared our staff list with theirs this afternoon, your card was among the older ones that the new readers no longer recognize. I would not want you to arrive at a locked door if you plan to come in while the front desk is unstaffed.

The replacement is straightforward, although it must be done in person: the management office on the ground floor will reissue the card while you wait, provided you bring your current card and a photo ID. Could you let me know by the end of today whether you are able to stop by tomorrow before they close, so that I can tell them to expect you?
Regards
